title: Jonathan Blow – If AI solved coding, why is my software still the same? [video]
titleZh: Jonathan Blow – If AI solved coding, why is my software still the same? [video]
author: helloplanets
relevanceReason: 命中 1 个 AI/科技关键词。

comments.author: Overdrivr
comments.textRawHtml: It's because the hard part of making software is not coding, but deciding what's worth building (even with LLMs), appropriately modelling the problem and designing the solution (at a conceptual, architectural level). And there has been strictly zero progress on this and IMO this isn't something LLMs are strucurally capable of doing.

children.author: glimshe
children.textRawHtml:
I remember that back in the 80s, when I was still deciding what I wanted to do when I grew up, there was a distinction between a "programmer" and a "systems analyst".

The systems analyst analyzed the problem that needed to be solved and designed a solution involving a computer, including system modules, inputs, outputs, etc.

The programmer, supposedly a lower paid profession, transformed that into Computer code. I remember someone telling me that wasn't the best choice and that I should become a "systems analyst". They wore the better suits.

My college even offered a shorter, cheaper degree for people who just wanted to be "programmers".

I think this distinction still survives in government labor statistics.

Perhaps we came full circle with LLMs partially killing the "programmer" job.

children.author: xorcist
children.textRawHtml:
We might be the same generation, I recognize the two roles. What I also remember is just empirically how much better the "programmers" were at doing the "system analysts" job. Way, way better. Then we stopped educating system analysts and now the job title is not heard of anymore.

I regularly meet (recently examined) people who are trained "software architects". Common among them is that they are often delay projects championing their pet idea, sometimes bringing negative value to the project. The best programmers are just so much better software architects also. So I expect history to repeat at this point.

children.author: EarthBlues
children.textRawHtml:
Programmers are better architects because their decisions are continually informed by experience from the "sharp end" of the system.  LLMs don't really have experiences, I dont think its the same.
Our profession will likely shake out a lot of people in the coming years.  What will be left may not be a classic "systems analyst" or "architect" role. I think the people who stay in this field will have to move both up and down the abstraction stack simultaneously -- our job will become a lot more "real", physical, relational, risk-oriented.  I dont think there's good reason to believe LLMs can supply the need for prudence in the fields where software is deployed.

children.author: ctkhn
children.textRawHtml: You do need to stay in touch with the sharp end to stay sharp yourself. I've had a lot of managers and directors in my career who as they have moved up in companies, longer write any code, and seem to not really get how our systems work even though they are in charge. I had a few managers in the past who were "non technical" and had never written code in their life, and they were the absolute worst of the bunch. children.author: saltcured
children.textRawHtml:
In my opinion, a lot of that "no longer getting it" is because of the social/fashion trends that continually disrupt programming.

You don't forget CS concepts so easily, but all the syntactic tricks of new language variants and working set vocabulary of APIs, data formats, and frameworks keeps churning away from whatever you last had contacted in a real, hands-on way.

It is fascinating, wondering where this is going as programmers turn into their own middle managers on top of agents. Particularly, the school who claim that you don't really need to understand all the code and instead treat it like a black-box experiment. If this fad takes over the main stage, then everyone becomes one of those less technical managers.

But, in this new scenario, there is no human in the loop to inject judgement calls and "manage up" anymore. There is no programmer culture except the models and agents, which don't really have the same social connections to drive a programming culture. What will happen? A culture per agent product? Per enterprise client of the agent vendor? Per agent operator? Per codebase?

children.author: ohyes
children.textRawHtml: I don’t think we get new things. Right now they’re great at popular languages and frameworks. If those change? There’s not enough training data. It could generate the data and train itself but where’s the incentive. It certainly can’t learn a new language right away the way even a junior programmer can. It will constantly hallucinate and not improve.

children.author: torginus
children.textRawHtml:
Weird how these fads just disappear overnight, 1984 style.

About half a year ago I noticed there were no people called 'Agile something' at our org, so I asked about it. They looked at me like I was a space alien. I remember, it was like 3 years ago that management bet the house on 'Agile transformation' talking about how Agile practices are the bread and butter of a good organization.

Now they're talking about AI the same way.

children.author: somesortofthing
children.textRawHtml: "Don't try to completely plan out huge software projects and commit to rigid delivery timelines in advance," "Split work into manageable tasks", "Run daily meetings to keep managers(and sometimes coworkers) in the decision loop and surface blockers", etc. are iron laws everyone instinctively recognizes are there for a reason. The explicit framework fell away because its principles became ubiquitous - nobody needs to hire Agile™ consultants to tell their SWEs and managers to do things the way they've been doing them for their whole career.

children.author: ElevenLathe
children.textRawHtml:
You say this like its universal, but my ostensibly Agile org is currently planning the work we will be delivering Q1 of 2028 because that is how long our [proposed work] -> [approved work] -> [finished work] pipeline runs.

The memo has NOT gotten around, though AI now makes it easier to make all the various slide decks and schedule all the 50+ person meetings that power this process.

children.author: derefr
children.textRawHtml:
> Common among them is that they are often delay projects championing their pet idea, sometimes bringing negative value to the project.

Negative value to the project, perhaps; but if these "software architects" are kept around despite several rounds of this, it may be because they're providing positive value to the company, in terms of producing for the company a thing whose existence (no matter how flawed) serves as collateral for:

- the executive team, to show to investors, to convince them that they're acting strategically in the market; or

- the marketing team, to get breathless puff-piece articles written about the company, in places where dumb CTOs/CIOs who make IT buying decisions will read them. (Not necessarily to then buy the specific product that came out of that project — hopefully not, in fact! — but instead to remember the company itself the next time they're comparing vendors for something else);

- or the executive team again, this time to show to a potential acquirer, to convince the acquirer that their employees have a higher asset value for having a certain skill / experience with certain paradigms, that they gained working on this project.

Companies have spent collective billions (trillions?) of dollars on projects they know will go nowhere, just to be able to say they did a project that is made a certain way or does a certain thing or has certain certifications, and to have a shitty codebase they can pull out of their back pocket if needed to back that up. In all such cases, even if they need to present the product, the product will never be evaluated for its quality or for its fit-for-purpose-ness; so it doesn't matter that the project failed to produce something of quality or that is fit-for-purpose. It just matters that the project happened.

children.author: microtonal
children.textRawHtml:
The systems analyst analyzed the problem that needed to be solved and designed a solution involving a computer, including system modules, inputs, outputs, etc.

I think both definitions are still too narrow for what I do daily. I fully agree that we still need humans to decide what to build, how it should all fit together, etc.

But both definitions do not really take into account the huge social dimension of being a good (computer) engineer in a company. You have to translate requests from a wild variety of users into what this means for a system. You have to recognize and explain that what they need is not always what they think they need. You have to be able to say "no" to things. All these things are very hard for an LLM (reading humans, not literally following requests).

Then there are social aspects like building consensus within a project, building a user base of many people that are initially skeptical, using existing relations with people and other companies to slowly adopt what you are building, etc.

Programming used to be a large chunk of the work. I thoroughly enjoyed this aspect of the work when I was younger, but at some point I started enjoying system design and everything around it more. So in that sense, programming with LLMs is much nicer (though I still review every single line of code and often have to go through a couple of iterations because even Opus 5.5 often doesn't get it 'right' in the first take). But the remaining part of the work is extremely hard for an LLM to replace.

children.author: prmph
children.textRawHtml:
Then we have/had "Software Engineer", then "Software Architect", etc.

Words are just words. In tech especially, it seems anyone can call themselves whatever they want.

Someone who chooses to call themselves "programmer" can be more engineering-minded and see the big picture better than someone that calls themselves an engineer.

children.author: retwakm4
children.textRawHtml:
I prefer to call myself a programmer because I don't think we (as a class) consistently perform a lot of the types of duties (both ethical ones and just basic job performance ones) that would be required of a lot of engineering disciplines.

I also started out in systems programming and we still call ourselves programmers there, when there is a lot of systems "engineering" (aka trying not to blow up the system with your code running in supervisor state) going on. And there, a lot more attention paid to stuff like IEEE code of ethics, professional development, rigorous designs, etc.

So I'll keep to calling myself programmer amongst my non software engineering friends. It just seems more humble.

That being said, writing the code has like others have pointed out, never been the largest part of the job in my experience. So I can see how it may be confusing to some, especially software engineers. But to non software engineers I think they mostly get it...you are a software engineer trying not to imply some some sort of unearned intellectual superiority.
